newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - driving season elusive.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - driving season elusive.

text.p: Bullish gasoline traders may have their patience tested this week as the traditional "driving season" rally remains elusive in 1997.

Differentials for both New York Harbor and U.S. Gulf conventional barrels are expected to languish at their current levels, with high levels of domestic output and imports keeping a lid on price gains even as seasonal demand picks up, oil products traders said.

So far, the approach to the 1997 gasoline season has been a dud, with spot NYH conventional unleaded hovering at 58.9 cents a gallon late Friday, far short of the 73.20 cents commanded on the same day last year.
And USG conventional unleaded was selling for about 57.8 cents late Friday, a full ten cents shy of last year.

Although total U.S. gasoline stocks are 8.9 million barrels lower than last year's levels, which were then a record low, traders said the market has apparently grown more comfortable with the industry's propensity to run "just-in-time" inventories.
The exception to the generally soggy market is U.S. high octane reformulated gasolines, which spiked last week on rumors of refinery reformer problems and remained firm Monday.

"D2 (premium reformulated gasoline) doesn't go to 12 cents over the screen (futures) without someone having a reformer problem," said Tom Knight, a refined products trader at Fina Inc, the U.S. unit of Belgium's Petrofina SA.

Knight and other traders said rumors included a number of refineries -- Star Enterprises' Delaware City, Del., Mobil Corp Paulboro, N.J., the giant Exxon at Baytown, La., Citgo, Phillips and possibly Valero in the U.S. Gulf -- though none was substantiated.
Some traders suggested that the rumors emerged on the futures floor late last week and might have been started by traders looking to rescue paper positions.

Nevertheless, the differential on D2 made up 80 percent of the 5.00 cents-a-gallon rise that lifted outright prices to 74.50 cents a gallon last week. Gulf Coast V1, 93-octane premium conventional gasoline also was relatively firm.
Both market sectors are relatively thin and increasingly linked to imports of blendstocks, factors which would exacerbate price movements based on a sudden spike in demand, market players said.

Nizar Sharief, an industry analyst at Hornsby & Co in Houston, noted that a year-on-year comparison of American Petroleum Institute data shows a much greater reliance on blendstocks at the expense of finished gasoline imports.
"Only the MTBE and the blending components are saving the day," Sharief said. Blendstocks in the first quarter averaged 221,000 bpd, up from 53,000 bpd in the 1996 first quarter.

Some traders said the restart of Tosco Corp's refinery at Trainer, Penn., near Philadelphia is another factor likely to cap any gasoline rally. The plant, with a capacity of around 150,000 bpd, is expected to start up again around mid-May after being idle a year following a labor dispute.
